doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Toots Thielemans on the blindfold test
summary: Levy identifies Toots from a recording, describes meeting and sitting in with him, and Toots's dominant influence on chromatic jazz harmonica.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Okay I’ve got – I’ve got one more for you –
I can’t recognize the tune but it’s obviously Toots. Is it from that Brazilian project album or is it –
You are absolutely correct. It’s Toots with Quincy Jones from the album “Walking in Space.”

“Walking in Space.” Yeah. Oh Quincy loved Toots. I mean, and I got to meet Toots and play with him a few times too. And of course you know he played the chromatic with the button on it. And was very intrigued and kind of like puzzled by like why I was playing chromatically on a diatonic. But we got along real well. And yeah Toots was a genius, a musical genius who just so happened to play the harmonica and give his gifts to the instrument. But the thing about him musically was that he started on accordion and he also saw the harmonica as a keyboard. Yeah. So I discovered that the first time we met and I sat in with him when I was in my – maybe I was 30, 31 or something like that, in Chicago. So yeah, he was an incredible, incredible musician, an amazing harmonica player. And for jazz chromatic playing for about 30 or 40 years nobody who played jazz on chromatic had their own personality because his was so strong. It took a long time before chromatic jazz players started sounding different. Like Gregoire Maret and people like that who just sounded like a guy playing a chromatic harmonica instead of sounding like Toots.
